This is Gallery 1. Work out which operation made each copy, then try the quiz.
The Workshop has four levers: slide, turn, mirror and send a shape through its centre.
The information desk can point you to the galleries, the Workshop and the guided tour.
Look closely at the copies in Gallery 1. Can you name the symmetry operation that made each one?
I am collecting examples of translation, rotation, reflection and inversion. Which is your favourite?
Gallery 2 tells the story of how people discovered crystal symmetry. Read the timeline from south to north.
After Gallery 2, visit Gallery 3 to see crystal models, then continue north to the Portal Hall.

# Mirror Plaza
## Symmetry m · tier 1
A mirror plane (m) runs through the middle of this plaza, north to south.

# Twofold Yard
## Symmetry 2 · tier 1
A 2-fold rotation axis stands upright in the middle of this yard.

# Fourfold Tower
## Symmetry 4 · tier 1
A 4-fold rotation axis stands upright in the middle of this tower.

# Inversion Core
## Symmetry -1 · tier 1
An inversion centre (-1, say 'bar one') floats in the middle of this cube.

# Translation Hall
## Symmetry P1 · tier 1
This hall is a crystal: 27 identical boxes (unit cells) stacked 3 by 3 by 3.

# Twin Mirrors
## Symmetry mm2 · tier 2
Two mirror planes meet at right angles along the vertical line in the middle.

# Monoclinic Cube
## Symmetry 2/m · tier 2
A vertical 2-fold axis, plus a horizontal mirror plane perpendicular to it.

# Square Court
## Symmetry 4mm · tier 2
A 4-fold axis with mirror planes: two along the sides and two along the diagonals.

# Orthorhombic Cube
## Symmetry mmm · tier 2
Three mirror planes, all at right angles, each through the middle of a shoebox and parallel to one pair of its faces.

# Diagonal Cube
## Symmetry 3 · tier 3
A 3-fold axis runs along the long diagonal of this cube, from one corner to the opposite corner.

# Rotoinversion Room
## Symmetry -4 · tier 3
-4 (say 'bar four'): turn a quarter turn about the vertical axis, then invert through the centre.

# Bar-Three Room
## Symmetry -3 · tier 3
-3 (say 'bar three'): turn a third of a turn about the long diagonal of the cube, then invert through the centre.

# Kaleidoscope
## Symmetry m-3m · tier 3
The full symmetry of a cube: m-3m, the highest point symmetry a crystal can have.

# Impossible Room
## Symmetry 1 · tier 3
This room was meant to have a 6-fold axis. It cannot be built on a block grid.

# Screw Hall
## Symmetry P2_1 · tier 4
A 2_1 screw axis: turn half a turn about a vertical axis, then rise by half a unit cell.

# Glide Hall
## Symmetry Pa · tier 4
A glide plane: reflect in a vertical plane, then slide half a cell along it.

# Spiral Tower
## Symmetry P4_1 · tier 4
A 4_1 screw axis: a quarter turn about the vertical axis, then a rise of a quarter of a cell (here 2 blocks).

# Mystery Lab
## Symmetry ? · tier 4
This lab has a hidden symmetry. Build, look at the copies, and work out the point group.

# Free Lab
## Symmetry 1 · tier 4
Your lab. Build anything, then type /whatsymmetry to have the exact point group worked out.

# Mirror Tiles
## Symmetry pmm · tier 4
A floor pattern with plane group pmm: mirror lines in two directions at right angles, repeated in every cell.

# Glide Tiles
## Symmetry pgg · tier 4
Plane group pgg: glide lines in two directions and 2-fold rotation points, but no mirror lines at all.

# Pinwheel Tiles
## Symmetry p4 · tier 4
Plane group p4: 4-fold rotation points, repeated in every cell, and no mirrors or glides.

# Weave Tiles
## Symmetry p4g · tier 4
Plane group p4g: 4-fold rotation points with mirror lines and glide lines, but no mirror passes through a 4-fold point.

# MUSEUM OF CRYSTALS AND SYMMETRY
Welcome. The doors open with a click.

# Museum of Crystals and Symmetry
Crystals are atoms arranged in patterns that repeat. Symmetry is the language that describes those patterns, and this museum teaches it by letting you build with it.

West: the Workshop, with the Try-it Pad.   East: Visitor information, with Prism, the AI tutor.
North: Gallery 1, Four kinds of symmetry. Beyond it, Gallery 2, A history of crystallography, and Gallery 3, Crystals at the atomic scale.
Furthest north: the Portal Hall, with a portal to every symmetry world.

Type /tour for a ten-minute guided tour. Press I for your progress.

# The Try-it Pad
Make your own shape and see what each of the four moves does to it.

1. Pick a coloured block from the bar at the bottom of the screen (keys 1 to 8).
2. Build a small shape in the glass box on the left, marked YOUR SHAPE. Right-click places a block, left-click removes one. A good first shape: three blocks in a row, a tower of two blocks on top of one end, and one block sticking out sideways at the other end.
3. Hit one of the four levers in front of the boxes with a left-click: T slides your shape, R turns it half a turn, M makes its mirror image, I sends it through its centre point.
4. A question appears: if you could pick the copy up and turn it any way you like, could it look exactly like your shape? Answer, then look at the box on the right, marked COPY.

T and R always give a copy you could turn back to match. M and I give a mirror twin, like your left and right hands, which no turning can match. Unless your shape is symmetric itself: try a plain row of blocks with M.

# How to explore
Walk with W A S D and look with the mouse. Press K to fly and J to go fast.
Press T or / to type a command, I for your progress board.

/quiz answers questions that unlock the next tier.
/explain repeats what the place you are in is about.
/step shows each copy appear, with the name of the operation.
/byhand lets you place the copies yourself.
/whatsymmetry works out the symmetry of what you built.
/tour is a ten-minute guided tour.

Every block in your inventory is free.

# Words to know
Symmetry operation: a move that leaves an object indistinguishable from how it started.
Symmetry element: the point, line or plane an operation acts about (centre, axis, mirror plane).
n-fold rotation axis: rotating by 360/n degrees leaves the object unchanged. Written n (2, 3, 4, 6).
Mirror plane: written m. It swaps left- and right-handed shapes.
Inversion centre: written -1 (say 'bar one'). Sends (x, y, z) to (-x, -y, -z).
Rotoinversion: a rotation followed by an inversion, written -n (-1, -3, -4, -6). A mirror is the same as -2.
Point group: the set of all symmetry operations of an object that leave one point fixed.
Order of a group: how many operations it contains. One block in a general position makes that many copies.
Hermann-Mauguin symbol: the standard short name of a group, such as 4mm or 2/m. '/' means 'with a mirror perpendicular to'.

# Gallery 1: Four kinds of symmetry
Each of the four displays, A to D, shows the same small shape twice: the original on the left, and on the right a copy made by one move.

1. Stand in front of the displays, facing them. A is on the left, D on the right.
2. For each display, compare the copy with the original. Was it just slid along? Turned around? Is it a mirror image? Or was every block sent through a centre point to the opposite side?
3. Press T, type /quiz and press Enter. Answer which move made each copy.

Answer all five questions correctly and the first worlds in the Portal Hall open for building.

# A history of crystallography
For three centuries, people have asked why crystals have flat faces and sharp angles. The answer, symmetry and the repeating lattice, grew step by step. Walk along the timeline.

# 1669  Nicolas Steno
Studying quartz, Steno found that the angles between matching faces are always the same, however large or misshapen the crystal: the first law of crystallography.

# 1784  René-Just Haüy
Haüy proposed that crystals are built from tiny identical units stacked in rows, which explained why calcite always breaks into smaller rhombohedra: the first idea of a unit cell.

# 1830  Johann Hessel
Hessel showed that the outward shapes of crystals can have only 32 kinds of symmetry: the 32 crystal classes, or point groups. 25 of them fit the block grid of this world.

# 1848  Auguste Bravais
Bravais showed that there are exactly 14 different kinds of lattice in three dimensions, now called the Bravais lattices.

# 1891  Evgraf Fedorov and Arthur Schoenflies
Working independently, they counted every way that symmetry operations and lattices can combine in three dimensions: 230 space groups.

# 1912  Max von Laue
With Walter Friedrich and Paul Knipping, Laue shone X-rays through a crystal and recorded a pattern of spots, showing that crystals are regular arrays of atoms. Nobel Prize in Physics, 1914.

# 1913  William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg
Father and son used X-ray diffraction to work out the first crystal structures, among them rock salt and diamond. Nobel Prize in Physics, 1915.

# 1935  The International Tables
The first International Tables for crystallography were published, using the Hermann-Mauguin symbols, such as 4mm and m-3m, that this museum uses.

# 1953  The double helix of DNA
X-ray images of DNA, including Photo 51 by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, helped James Watson and Francis Crick propose the double helix. A helix has screw symmetry.

# 1964  Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin
Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using X-ray crystallography to work out the structures of important molecules, including penicillin and vitamin B12.

# 1982  Dan Shechtman
Shechtman saw a diffraction pattern with 5-fold symmetry, which no periodic crystal can have. Quasicrystals are ordered but not periodic. Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2011.

# 2014  International Year of Crystallography
UNESCO's International Year of Crystallography marked a century of X-ray crystallography.

# Haüy's idea, in blocks
Identical cubes, stacked, make an octahedron with stepped faces. From far away the steps vanish and the faces look flat.

# Crystals at the atomic scale
Each model is a real crystal, one block per atom, with a gap between atoms so you can see inside.

Many of them share the cube's point group m-3m, yet their atoms are arranged differently: the space group tells them apart.

Punch the gold clue crystal in front of each model to answer a question about it.

# The Portal Hall
Each portal leads to a world with one symmetry group. Whatever you build there is copied by every operation of the group.

Tier 1: one operation at a time.  Tier 2: combining operations.  Tier 3: three dimensions.  Tier 4: lattices, space groups and floor patterns.

Worlds above your tier can be visited but not built in. Punch a portal to travel; every world has a portal back.

# PORTAL HALL
To the symmetry worlds

# PORTAL HALL
To the symmetry worlds

# Copper
Copper: atoms at the corners and the face centres of every cubic cell. This is called face-centred cubic. Each atom touches 12 others: one of the two closest ways to pack equal spheres. Space group Fm-3m.

# Iron
Iron at room temperature: atoms at the corners and at the centre of every cubic cell. This is called body-centred cubic. Each atom has 8 nearest neighbours, along the cube diagonals. Space group Im-3m.

# Rock salt
Rock salt, sodium chloride: sodium (purple) and chloride (green) alternate along every row, in all three directions. Each ion has 6 neighbours of the other kind. Space group Fm-3m: the lattice is face-centred cubic, like copper's.

# Caesium chloride
Caesium chloride: chloride (green) at the cube corners, caesium (blue) at the cube centre. It looks body-centred, but the centre holds a different ion, so the lattice is primitive cubic: space group Pm-3m.

# Perovskite
Strontium titanate: titanium (white) at the cube centre, oxygen (red) at the face centres, strontium (green) at the corners. Each titanium sits inside an octahedron of 6 oxygens. Many materials share this arrangement, called the perovskite structure. Space group Pm-3m.

# Diamond
Diamond: every carbon atom bonds to 4 others at the corners of a tetrahedron. Space group Fd-3m. The point symmetry at each carbon atom is -43m, the symmetry of a tetrahedron.

Right-click the screen, or type /ask anywhere

# Fluorite: an octahedron
Fluorite crystals often grow as cubes or octahedra, and they split along octahedron faces.

# Pyrite: a cube
Pyrite, 'fool's gold', often grows as near-perfect cubes, often with fine grooves across the faces.

# Halite: rock salt
Salt crystals are cubes, and they break into smaller cubes. See their atoms in Gallery 3.

# What symmetry? 4
A quarter turn about the post leaves this sculpture the same. It has no mirror: its mirror image would turn the other way.

# What symmetry? -1
Every block has a partner straight through the centre point, the same distance away on the other side. No turn and no mirror leaves it the same: only this inversion.
